The 3 gut microbial species recognized as being depleted in patients with fatal cirrhosis are A. muciniphila [24,25], R. intestinalis [26,27], and R. lactatiformans [28,29], and they are known to have beneficial health effects, especially in patients with liver diseases.

We found significant differences in fecal metabolites be tween healthy controls and cirrhosis patients, similar to the findings of a previous study of blood [30]. Overall, 5 metabolites with cirrhosis-dependent increases and decreases showed significantly high diagnostic ability, although the individual AUROCs were high for cirrhosis-dependent decreased metabolites. The 3-Indole propionic acid protects against liver injury by inhibiting NF-κB signaling, boosting the production of proinflammatory cytokines, and hindering hepatic fibrosis by suppressing the activation of hepatic stellate cells [31], and butyrate regulates the LKB1-AMPK-Insig signaling pathway to reduce hepatic injury [32] in addition to other health-promoting effects [33,34]. Another decreased metabolite, stercobilin, is a fecal pigment that is metabolized by gut bacteria, and increases in this metabolite in feces and plasma are related to inflammation [35]. However, its depletion in feces is related to autism [36]; therefore, further investigations are required to establish its strong relationship with cirrhosis. Among metabolites increased in cirrhosis, Indole-3-lactic acid is a gut microbe produced Indole intermediate metabolites that can regulate T-cell-controlled immunomodulation [37,38].

text:

Among metabolites increased in cirrhosis, Indole-3-lactic acid is a gut microbe produced Indole intermediate metabolites that can regulate T-cell-controlled immunomodulation [37,38]. Thus, increased excretion of Indole-3-lactic acid in feces can be related to decreased Tcell-regulated immunomodulation and linked to cirrhosis progression. The other 2 metabolites, palmitoylcarnitine, are intermediate metabolites of fatty acid metabolism and are correlated with liver diseases [39,40] and N6,N6,N6-trimethyl-L-lysine is an intermediate of lysine degradation and is related to liver and cardiac diseases [30].

The significant finding of this study is the correlation between hallmark clinical biomarkers of cirrhosis and the identified excretory microbial and metabolic biomarkers. Compared with metabolic biomarkers, clinical biomarkers and microbial markers exhibited superior correlations, particularly with MELD score [41], hemostatic markers [42], AST [43], conjugated bilirubin levels [44], GGT [45], and albumin [46], which are considered the most valuable prognostic tools for determining the severity of compensated to decompensated cirrhosis. This remarkable correlation with hallmark clinical biomarkers of cirrhosis and notably high AUROCs values make these noninvasive microbial biomarkers excellent substitutes for biomarkers that require invasive clinical tests. Furthermore, metabolic markers that are reduced in patients with cirrhosis are strongly correlated with clinical markers, whereas metabolic markers are increased in patients with cirrhosis.

Furthermore, metabolic markers that are reduced in patients with cirrhosis are strongly correlated with clinical markers, whereas metabolic markers are increased in patients with cirrhosis. Hence, metabolic biomarkers can complement microbial biomarkers, and both provide a good experimental framework for discovering the pathophysiology of decomposition in cirrhosis.

Moreover, the associations of decreased microbial and metabolic markers with cirrhosis were greater than those of cirrhosis-enriched microbial and metabolic markers. These findings suggest that cirrhosis-dependent decreases in gut microbial species are more relevant than cirrhosis-enriched species. Five species (R. cacicola, R. intestinalis, R. inulinivorans, F. prausnitzii, and E. ventriosum) are known butyrate-producing bacteria [33] and are strongly negatively correlated with butyrate. Species such as R. intestinalis and F. prausnitzii are known for their ability to repair the gut barrier, ameliorate inflammation through increased production of anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL10 and IL22), suppress pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL17 and IFNγ), and improve energy metabolism [26,47].

Empirical data from the scientific literature suggest that the gut microbiome influences various immunological, metabolic and molecular pathways through microbe-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs) and pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs). It exerts its effects through its metabolites such as: short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), Indole and tryptophan metabolism-associated metabolites [48], choline metabolites (TMA and TMAO), bile acid, and byproducts of fermentation.

It exerts its effects through its metabolites such as: short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), Indole and tryptophan metabolism-associated metabolites [48], choline metabolites (TMA and TMAO), bile acid, and byproducts of fermentation. Thus, gut microbiome alterations are crucial because they are connected with metabolic shifts that lead to altered physiological pathways that either deteriorate or improve liver health, accordingly changing the clinical and immunological markers related to the liver [49,50]. Consequently, increased liver cirrhosis severity in the gut is decisive, and this correlation strengthens the gut microbiome and cirrhosis progression and encourages the use of noninvasive microbial biomarkers as robust prognostic tools in patients with decompensated cirrhosis. This study also demonstrated the significance of cirrhosis-dependent decreases in the gut microbiome, which can be directly linked to metabolic profiles and can ameliorate the pathophysiological pathways involved in cirrhosis progression. Thus, the combination of these noninvasive microbial biomarkers for the early detection of decompensation in patients with cirrhosis and the use of new generations of probiotics to limit the progression of the disease could improve mortality related to ACLF.

Along with substantial positive outcomes, this trial also has several limitations. Further investigation through future preclinical and clinical trials is necessary to improve our understanding of the role of gut microbes and metabolites as biomarkers in liver cirrhosis and associated complications.

Further investigation through future preclinical and clinical trials is necessary to improve our understanding of the role of gut microbes and metabolites as biomarkers in liver cirrhosis and associated complications. However, this current clinical trial has successfully identified and established correlations between several fecal microbial and metabolite biomarkers and clinical markers, nonetheless, the pathophysiological connections within these intra-correlations need extensive exploration. Therefore, preclinical and clinical trials are essential for validating associations between these markers and for the establishment of robust pathophysiological mechanisms related to the progression of liver cirrhosis severity. Despite having adequate patient numbers to identify the biomarkers, validation of these biomarkers is vital to ensure their accuracy, reliability, and clinical utility. Therefore, multicentric larger population-based clinical trials are required to determine the clinical relevance of these identified microbial and metabolic biomarkers corresponding to the progression of liver cirrhosis severity.

Since this was a cross-sectional observational trial, temporal variation in the gut microbial ecology and fecal metabolic profile as liver cirrhosis progresses is a major concern. These temporal variations are pivotal indicators of the progression of liver cirrhosis and its complications: thus, it is essential to measure these differences in the fecal microbiome and metabolites.

title: Microbiome and metabolomics reveal the effect of gut microbiota on liver regeneration of fatty liver disease
text: Epidemiological investigations have revealed the increasing global prevalence of metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD), and hepatic steatosis is known to be associated with an impaired regenerative capacity and poor postoperative prognosis after partial hepatectomy (PHx). Currently, there is substantial evidence for the correlation between MAFLD progression and the gut microbial community. However, limited data are available on the dynamic changes in the gut microbiota during the course of liver regeneration in MAFLD, as well as its metabolic regulatory mechanisms.

title: Microbiome and metabolomics reveal the effect of gut microbiota on liver regeneration of fatty liver disease
text: Significant alterations in gut microbiome and liver metabolomics were observed in high-fat diet induced MAFLD mice undergoing PHx. Time-series analysis provides an intuitive approach for demonstrating the dynamic fluctuations of datasets over time. The microbiota and metabolites were divided into separate clusters according to the different abundance trends over time, and those that were consistent with the liver regeneration rate were selected for further investigation. Spearman correlation analysis was used to screen out bacterial candidates that affected MAFLD liver regeneration through metabolic pathways. Notably, Akkermansia appeared as the top species in the screened microbial cluster and was positively correlated with TCA cycle metabolites. We then confirmed the ability of Akkermansia muciniphila to suppress hepatic inflammation and lipid accumulation and promote post-PHx liver regeneration in MAFLD mice.

title: Microbiome and metabolomics reveal the effect of gut microbiota on liver regeneration of fatty liver disease
section: Implications of all the available evidence
text: This study combined microbiome and metabolomic profiling to screen specific bacterial targets that may affect liver regeneration in MAFLD. We provide a theoretical basis for promoting postoperative MAFLD liver regeneration by modulating gut microbiota with probiotic supplementation.

title: Microbiome and metabolomics reveal the effect of gut microbiota on liver regeneration of fatty liver disease
text:
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) encompasses a spectrum of pathological conditions, from simple steatosis to steatohepatitis without the influence of secondary causes, and can develop into non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NASH) and cirrhosis.1,2 In most epidemiological studies, the global prevalence of NAFLD is estimated to be 25% and continues to increase in parallel with the worldwide obesity epidemic.3 NAFLD is known to have a close correlation with obesity and often coexists with metabolic comorbidities.3,4 In a recent consensus publication by Eslam et al., it was proposed that NAFLD should be reclassified as metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD), which is considered a more suitable and inclusive terminology.5

Partial hepatectomy (PHx) is an effective treatment for a range of liver diseases, including benign and malignant tumours, intrahepatic duct calculi, and abscesses. Hepatic steatosis is known as a risk factor for poor prognosis after PHx, and fat accumulation disrupts hepatocyte homeostasis, which may result in increased postoperative mortality and complications.6,7 Clinically, approximately over 20% of patients requiring liver resection present with varying severity of steatosis.6 Notably, individuals with moderate to severe hepatic steatosis demonstrate significantly impaired liver regenerative capacity after PHx, and clinicians should exercise caution when evaluating the extent of liver resection.7, 8, 9, 10 In murine experiments, numerous studies have also documented the inhibitory effects of steatosis on liver regeneration in both genetic and diet-induced MAFLD models.11, 12, 13 Therefore, identifying intervention targets to promote liver regeneration after PHx in patients with MAFLD is meaningful.

title: Microbiome and metabolomics reveal the effect of gut microbiota on liver regeneration of fatty liver disease
text:
so documented the inhibitory effects of steatosis on liver regeneration in both genetic and diet-induced MAFLD models.11, 12, 13 Therefore, identifying intervention targets to promote liver regeneration after PHx in patients with MAFLD is meaningful.

The gut–liver axis denotes bidirectional crosstalk between the gut and liver, encompassing the reciprocal regulation of metabolites, microbial antigens, nutrients, and bile acids.14 The pivotal role of the gut–liver axis in the pathogenesis of hepatic steatosis is well established.15, 16, 17 Multiple mechanisms link microbial dysbiosis and MAFLD, including choline deficiency, increased intestinal permeability, and alterations in short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) synthesis and bile acid composition.15 In addition, the complex relationship between gut microbiota and liver regeneration has attracted much attention. As early as 1985, Cornell et al. discovered that gut sterilization impaired liver regeneration after 67% liver resection in rats.18 Liver regeneration is accompanied by significant metabolic remodeling,19 and rapid advances in metabolomic techniques in recent years have offered a novel perspective on the mechanisms of gut microbes in diseases and physiological processes. Liu and colleagues have demonstrated relevant associations between hepatic gene expression profiles and liver metabolism with changing gut microbiota during liver regeneration, where gut-derived metabolites, such as SCFAs and bile acids, play important roles.20 However, there is currently a lack of studies investigating the impact of gut microbiota on postoperative liver regeneration in MAFLD as well as the potential metabolic mechanisms involved.

In this study, we employed a combination of gut microbiome and liver metabolomics to elucidate the role of the gut microbiota in postoperative liver regeneration in MAFLD and preliminarily explored the underlying metabolic mechanisms. We also identified and validated a potential probiotic, Akkermansia muciniphila (A. muciniphila), which may be beneficial for facilitating postoperative recovery in obese individuals with MAFLD (Fig. S1).

Liver tissues were pulverised in liquid nitrogen and dissolved in 80% methanol. After incubating on ice for 5 min, samples were centrifuged (15,000 g, 4 °C, 20 min) and diluted to 53% methanol concentration, and centrifuged again (15,000 g, 4 °C, 20 min). The supernatant was collected and injected into the liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) system for analysis.

The UHPLC-MS/MS analysis was conducted using the Vanquish UHPLC system (Thermo Scientific) and Orbitrap Q ExactiveTM HF mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific). Samples were injected into a Hypesil Gold column (100 × 2.1 mm, 1.9 μm) using a 12-min linear gradient at a temperature of 40 °C (0.2 mL/min). For positive polarity mode, Eluent A (0.1% FA in water) and eluent B (methanol) were used, and for negative polarity mode, eluent A (5 mM ammonium acetate, pH 9.0) and eluent B (methanol)were used. The solvent gradient was performed with 2% B, 1.5 min; 2–85% B, 3 min; 85–100% B, 10 min; 100–2% B, 10.1 min; 2% B, 12 min. Then, the Q ExactiveTM HF mass spectrometer was operated with a sheath gas flow rate of 35 psi, spray voltage of 3.5 kV, and capillary temperature of 320 °C. Raw data were imported into Compound Discoverer 3.1 (CD3.1, Thermo Scientific) for peak detection and alignment. Statistical analyses were performed using Python (version 2.7.6) and R (version R-3.4.3).

The metabolites were annotated using the KEGG (https://www.genome.jp/kegg/pathway.html) and LIPID MAPS (http://www.lipidmaps.org/) database.

text: Male C57BL/6J mice aged 5 weeks (weight 20 ± 2 g) were fed a HFD (60% kcal fat) for 12 weeks before 50% PHx (Fig. 1A). No significant difference in Masson staining was detected in mice fed with the HFD for 12 weeks, suggesting the absence of notable fibrosis (Fig. 1E). To assess the regeneration capacity of the fatty liver, HFD mice were randomly allocated to five groups, and all subjected to 50% PHx. Liver regeneration was continuously monitored for 7 days after surgery (Fig. 2A). The liver-to-body weight ratio increased continuously, and the growth rate peaked on the third day post-PHx before declining (Fig. 2B). Immunostaining for PCNA indicated that the proliferative capacity of hepatocytes increased from day 2 and peaked on day 3 after PHx (Fig. 2C). Consistent with the immunoblot results, liver sections from the day 3 group showed a significantly higher percentage of Ki-67 positive cells, suggesting enhanced cell proliferation (Fig. 2D and E). Serum levels of ALT and AST, specific markers of liver injury, transiently increased on the first day after hepatectomy, whereas the concentrations of DBIL, TBIL, and TBA exhibited an overall upward trend, indicating fluctuations in liver function. Serum lipid levels, including TG and TC, showed a continuous decline (Fig. 2F). It is well established that the peak rate of liver regeneration in rodents typically occurs within the first 1–2 days after PHx.23 These data demonstrated that liver regeneration and cell proliferation in HFD mice occurred with a delayed timeline, with the peak on the third day after PHx.Fig.

title: Microbiome and metabolomics reveal the effect of gut microbiota on liver regeneration of fatty liver disease
section: The gut microbial communities altered after PHx in HFD mice
text: Alterations in the intestinal microbiota associated with liver regeneration were characterised by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing of faecal samples. The rarefaction analysis (Fig. S2A) and species accumulation curve (Fig. S2B) confirmed the adequacy of the sampling efforts. The bacterial diversity of the microbiome was assessed, with both the Chao1 and Shannon indices showing an abrupt reduction, followed by a gradual recovery over time after PHx (Fig. 3A). Beta-diversity analysis was visualized based on non-metric multi-dimensional scaling (NMDS) to measure differences between group. Throughout the regeneration process, the overall microbiota structure diverged significantly and then progressively shifted towards the initial community observed on day 0 (Fig. 3B, Fig. S2C). The relative abundance of the gut microbiota at multiple levels was quantified to identify the characteristic microbes in each phase. At the phylum level, the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio consistently reduced and began to recover in the late phase (Fig. S2D and E). The microbiome composition at the genus level also varied with the time points in the regeneration process, and the top 14 bacteria with the highest relative abundance in each group are shown in Fig. 3C. In particular, Dubosiella, Escherichia-Shigella, Bacteroides, Akkermansia, and Muribaculaceae showed pronounced peaks. Dubosiella (20.29%) was the most abundant bacteria in MAFLD mice fed with the HFD. After PHx, Escherichia-Shigella (68.19%) and Bacteroides (29.32%) became the dominant bacteria on the first and second postoperative days, respectively, whereas Muribaculaceae dominated in the late stages of liver regeneration (42.94% on day 5 and 28.37% on day 7).

text:
To further elucidate the changes in gut microbiota during the process of liver regeneration, the longitudinal analysis was conducted. We used the R package TimeSeriesExperiment to analyse the microbiome at the amplicon sequence variants (ASV) level for visualisation and dataset analysis. A total of 6 clusters were obtained, each of which exhibited a distinct trend (Fig. 4A). Bacteria in Cluster 1 exhibited consistent upregulation from the fifth day post-surgery, whereas bacteria in Cluster 5 were monotonically downregulated from the outset. Notably, the bacteria in Clusters 2 and 4 showed significant downregulation and upregulation, respectively, on the second day after PHx. Cluster 3 bacteria were upregulated on the third day. Finally, bacteria in Cluster 6 experienced a slight initial downregulation on the first day, followed by a monotonic upregulation (Fig. 4A). Of these, the line of Cluster 3 trended upward on day 2 and peaked on day 3, which highly corresponded with the liver regeneration curve of MAFLD mice (Fig. 2B–E), indicating a potential positive association between these bacteria and liver regeneration in MAFLD.

title: Microbiome and metabolomics reveal the effect of gut microbiota on liver regeneration of fatty liver disease
section: The alteration of liver metabolome after PHx
text:
Liver regeneration involves substantial metabolic remodeling,19 while gut bacteria-derived metabolites can exert a regulatory function in the liver through the gut–liver axis. We conducted metabolomic profiling of liver samples collected from HFD mice at different time points after PHx using untargeted LC-MS/MS. A total of 584 metabolites were identified for positive mode, and 339 metabolites for negative mode. Pearson correlation coefficient served as a quality control to assess the stability and repeatability of the metabolomic data (Fig. S3B). The principal component analysis (PCA) plot showed a separation trend among the groups. As shown in Fig. 5A, a distinct separation was observed between the day 0 and day 1 groups, with subsequent convergence towards the day 0 group as time progressed, indicating significant alterations in hepatic metabolite composition. Furthermore, hierarchical clustering analysis (HCA) of the metabolites showed distinct clusters and a discernible pattern of initial separation, followed by convergence towards the D0 group (Fig. S3C).Fig. 5Alteration of metabolic profiles in HFD mice after PHx. (C) Lipid annotation based on Lipidmaps database in positive ion mode. (D) Longitudinal analysis of the Metabolomics by Mfuzz. (E) Network-level correlations of metabolites in cluster 6. The functional annotations of the identified metabolites were analysed using the KEGG and LIPID MAPS databases to gain deeper insights into their classification and functional properties (Fig. 5B–C, Fig. S3D and E).

The functional annotations of the identified metabolites were analysed using the KEGG and LIPID MAPS databases to gain deeper insights into their classification and functional properties (Fig. 5B–C, Fig. S3D and E). The enriched KEGG pathways encompassed lipid metabolism, amino acid metabolism, cofactors and vitamins metabolism, nucleotide metabolism, and carbohydrate metabolism. Several lipid metabolites closely related to the gut microbiota such as bile acids and fatty acids (FAs) were annotated using Lipidmaps (Fig. 5C). The results revealed that liver regeneration induced extensive alterations in the liver metabolism in MAFLD mice post-PHx.

title: Microbiome and metabolomics reveal the effect of gut microbiota on liver regeneration of fatty liver disease
section: Longitudinal analysis of liver metabolomics during liver regeneration
text:
To better comprehend the temporal dynamics of the metabolome dataset during liver regeneration, we utilised time-series clustering analysis via Mfuzz26 to categorise all 923 metabolites into 8 patterns (Cluster 1,..., Cluster 8) (Fig. 5D). The metabolites in Clusters 3 and 7 exhibited consistent and continuous upregulation and downregulation, respectively, after PHx. During the first and second days, metabolites in Cluster 4 were substantially upregulated, while Clusters 5 and 8 were downregulated. The metabolites in Clusters 1 and 6 manifested notable downregulation and upregulation, respectively, only between the second and third days. Additionally, the metabolites in Cluster 2 exhibited an initial upregulation on the first day, followed by a sustained decline until the third day before commencing the recovery phase. From these results, we concluded that liver metabolism underwent dynamic changes at certain points (Fig. 5D).

Furthermore, we identified metabolites in Cluster 6 as potential candidates implicated in the regulation of liver regeneration, given that their peak expression appeared on day 3 post PHx (the period of the fastest liver regeneration in HFD mice) (Fig. 2B–E). Cluster 6 comprised 96 metabolites primarily involved in the citrate cycle, pyrimidine metabolism, purine metabolism, primary bile acid biosynthesis, and glycerophospholipid metabolism (Table S2). Additionally, we visually presented a metabolite correlation network for Cluster 6; those with strong correlations (cor >0.7) were shown in Fig. 5E.

title: Microbiome and metabolomics reveal the effect of gut microbiota on liver regeneration of fatty liver disease
section: Relationships of gut microbiome and liver metabolomics
text: The crosstalk between the gut microbiome and liver metabolism plays an essential role in MAFLD pathogenesis.15 A series of gut bacteria were positively or negatively correlated with mouse phenomes and serum levels of liver function markers, lipids, bilirubin, and bile acid in HFD mice underwent PHx (Fig. S4). To investigate the potential connections between liver regeneration-altered microbes and metabolites, we performed a correlation analysis on two clusters selected through time-series analysis (Cluster 3 of the microbiome and Cluster 6 of the metabolome), considering the resemblance of their patterns of change with the liver regeneration curve. Spearman correlation analysis revealed that among the top 10 bacteria with the highest relative abundance, Parabacteroides, Blautia, Shinella, Akkermansia, Lachnoclostridium, and Eubacterium_coprostanoligenes_group were closely correlated with the metabolites (Fig. 6A). The names of metabolites corresponding to their respective IDs are listed in Table S2. Specifically, a strong positive correlation was observed between Blautia and guanosine monophosphate (GMP). Parabacteroides and Shinella exhibited positive correlations with citric acid and α-ketoglutaric acid (α-KG) (P < 0.05). Eubacterium_coprostanoligenes_group had a close relationship with dl-glutamine and d-α-hydroxyglutaric acid (D-2HG) (P < 0.01).Fig. 6Spearman correlation analysis and shotgun metagenomic sequencing. It is of notice that the abundance of Akkermansia, the dominant bacterium of Cluster 3, showed a significant positive correlation with citric acid, α-KG, D-2HG, dl-glutamine, and N-[4-(diethylamino) phenyl]-N′-phenylurea (P < 0.05) (Fig. 6A). The majority of these metabolites were closely associated with the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. Both citric acid and α-KG are key intermediates in the TCA cycle, while glutamine is known to enter the TCA cycle via ɑ-KG and serves as a source of NADPH.27 D-2HG is also a mitochondrial metabolite derived from α-ketoglutarate.28 The TCA cycle is indispensable for aerobic glycolysis and provides ATP, lipids, and nonessential amino acids for rapid cellular proliferation.29 Deranged ATP homeostasis is a critical factor in the impaired regeneration of fatty livers.6 Taken together, these six microbes were screened out to be potentially associated with MAFLD liver regeneration, and Akkermansia could be an attractive candidate that may function by affecting the TCA cycle.

title: Microbiome and metabolomics reveal the effect of gut microbiota on liver regeneration of fatty liver disease
section: A. muciniphila rescues liver regeneration in HFD mice
text:
Metagenome sequencing provides higher taxonomic resolution and offers functional insights into the microbial community.30 To identify liver regeneration-related bacterial species in MAFLD mice, we performed shotgun metagenomic sequencing of faecal samples from HFD mice before and on the third day after PHx, and found the upregulation of A. muciniphila, the most prominent species in the genus Akkermansia, at the species level (Fig. 6B). The important role of A. muciniphila in gut barrier protection and metabolic regulation is well recognised, and it is known as a next-generation probiotic (NGP). Studies have indicated a declined abundance of A. muciniphila in both mice and patients with MAFLD.31 Interestingly, our data showed an abnormal dominance of Akkermansia during the postoperative liver regeneration process, and the correlation analysis indicated a close association between Akkermansia and the TCA cycle. MetagenomeSeq analysis based on the KEGG database also revealed that the relative abundance of certain metabolic pathways, including carbohydrate metabolism, was higher on Day 3 compared to Day 0 (Fig. 6C). Consequently, A. muciniphila was considered for further validation to explore its potential in promoting postoperative liver regeneration in HFD-induced MAFLD mice via oral probiotic administration.

We validated the therapeutic effects of A. muciniphila in HFD and CD-HFD mouse models and observed similar effect in germ-free HFD mice. The AKK-treated group received oral administration of A. muciniphila for 4 weeks, whereas the control group (PBS-treated group) received an equal volume of PBS (Fig. 7A, Fig. S5A, and Fig. S6A). 16S rRNA gene sequencing indicated the colonization of A. muciniphila in AKK-treated HFD mice without antibiotic pre-treatment (Fig. S7).

title: Microbiome and metabolomics reveal the effect of gut microbiota on liver regeneration of fatty liver disease
text:
Despite the acknowledged significance of the gut microbiota in influencing MAFLD progression,32 limited information is available on the role of bacteria in post-hepatectomy regeneration in MAFLD. This study recorded the liver regeneration process and changes in liver function following PHx in mice with HFD-induced MAFLD. We demonstrated alterations in gut microbiota and liver metabolites over the course of post-PHx regeneration in mice with MAFLD. An analysis combining gut microbiota and liver metabolites indicated the potential underlying mechanisms by which the gut microbiota influence liver regeneration in obese mice. Furthermore, MAFLD mice treated with oral A. muciniphila exhibited substantial amelioration of lipid accumulation, inflammation, and liver regeneration. Our study provides new insights for facilitating postoperative recovery in patients with MAFLD undergoing liver resection.

Accumulating evidence has demonstrated that the gut microbiota can influence various physiological and pathophysiological processes in the liver, including steatosis and liver regeneration.15,20 Our study explored the potential involvement of the gut microbiota in the liver regeneration process in HFD-induced MAFLD. Significant changes in the gut microbiota were observed after PHx, with an overall recovery trend over time. Further analyses focused on the composition of gut microbiota in HFD-induced MAFLD mice. Dubosiella was found to be one of the most prominent bacteria (20.29%) in the faeces of MAFLD mice, consistent with previously published findings that Dubosiella was strongly correlated with NASH progression.33 After PHx, Escherichia-Shigella quickly became dominant (comprising 68.19% on the first day).

text: acteria (20.29%) in the faeces of MAFLD mice, consistent with previously published findings that Dubosiella was strongly correlated with NASH progression.33 After PHx, Escherichia-Shigella quickly became dominant (comprising 68.19% on the first day). Previous publications have shown a strong correlation between Shigella and inflammation,34 which supports our observations in the present work. Moreover, we noticed a temporary increase in the relative abundances of Muribaculaceae, Bacteroides, and Akkermansia. A community of strains including Muricbaculum has been reported to regulate lipid metabolism and stimulate liver regeneration,35,36 which may explain its persistent increase at the late stage of the liver regeneration process. Both Bacteroides and Akkermansia are closely associated with SCFAs production.31,37 In addition to their involvement in providing energy sources and regulating the host immune system, SCFAs generated by gut bacteria also play critical roles in lipid metabolism and liver regeneration through the gut–liver axis.35 Bacteroides is the main producer of propionate (one of the three major SCFAs in the human gut), and Akkermansia promotes the secretion of acetic, propionic, and butyric acids.31 Moreover, Akkermansia started to increase at the onset of liver regeneration in MAFLD mice and became the predominant bacterium (30.60%) when the regeneration rate peaked (on the third day after PHx). Akkermansia was further shown to be positively associated with liver regeneration rate in MAFLD mice in the time-series analysis of this study.

As a promising probiotic with therapeutic efficacy against inflammation, metabolic disorders, and liver diseases, the depletion of Akkermansia has previously been demonstrated in animals and humans with MAFLD.38 Therefore, the abnormally high levels of Akkermansia during liver regeneration in MAFLD mice in our study deserve further attention. Collectively, our study detected changes in gut microbiota during liver regeneration in MAFLD and may provide new bacterial targets for postoperative recovery.

There is an intricate metabolic interplay between the gut and liver.14,39 Numerous studies have been conducted to elucidate the mechanisms by which the gut microbiota regulate liver function and pathology.40 A recent study showed that SCFAs provided by gut bacteria were functionally important for the growth and proliferation of hepatocytes.35 To gain preliminary insights into the underlying metabolic mechanisms involved in the positive effect of microbiota on liver regeneration in MAFLD, we performed liver metabolomics and correlation analyses. The analysis revealed a close association between bacterial species abundance in Cluster 3 of the microbiome and metabolite abundance in Cluster 6. Six bacteria exhibited a positive relationship with the metabolomics. Blautia was positively related to GMP, while others were predominantly positively correlated with TCA cycle metabolites such as citric acid, α-KG, D-2HG, and glutamine. GMP, the ultimate product of purinosomes, provides material for DNA synthesis and cell proliferation.

text:
ly related to GMP, while others were predominantly positively correlated with TCA cycle metabolites such as citric acid, α-KG, D-2HG, and glutamine. GMP, the ultimate product of purinosomes, provides material for DNA synthesis and cell proliferation. The TCA cycle functions in the mitochondria, providing ATP and precursors for lipid, amino acid, and nucleotide synthesis for rapid cell proliferation.27 ATP plays a critical role in G1/S cell cycle transition during liver regeneration; however, a reduced ability to synthesise ATP due to mitochondrial dysfunction occurs in fatty hepatocytes.41,42 Our study identified the bacteria associated with MAFLD liver regeneration and their potential metabolic relevance.

Gut microbiota-based therapies such as probiotic therapy are believed to alleviate liver disease and promote liver regeneration.40 A. muciniphila, a strictly anaerobic bacterium abundant in the human intestinal microbiota, has been implicated in beneficial roles in MAFLD by restoring the gut barrier and gut–liver axis.31 However, there are no reports on the function and mechanism of action of A. muciniphila in liver regeneration. Therefore, we aimed to determine whether A. muciniphila played a direct causative role in enhancing cell proliferation after PHx in MAFLD. Compared with the control group, oral administration of A. muciniphila mitigated the development of MAFLD induced by HFD or CD-HFD, manifested by reduced rapidity of body/liver weight gain and decreased serum TG and ALT levels, which was consistent with observations in previous studies.43 Moreover, microbiota intervened with A. muciniphila accelerated hepatocyte proliferation in MAFLD mice.

text:
by reduced rapidity of body/liver weight gain and decreased serum TG and ALT levels, which was consistent with observations in previous studies.43 Moreover, microbiota intervened with A. muciniphila accelerated hepatocyte proliferation in MAFLD mice. The phenomenon was similarly observed in germ-free HFD mouse model, excluding the influence of other confounding factors. These findings suggested that in addition to its preventive effects on MAFLD, A. muciniphila can partially mitigate delayed liver regeneration in mice with MAFLD. However, whether the ability of A. muciniphila to promote liver regeneration is related to the alleviation of hepatic steatosis remains to be further investigated.

Nevertheless, some limitations of our study should be recognized. First, there is a disparity in the gut microbiota between humans and mice species; therefore, collection and further investigation of human specimens are warranted. Additionally, although we selected clusters that were positively correlated with liver regeneration, it is plausible that microbes negatively correlated with liver regeneration rates (potentially exerting harmful effects) could also be meaningful. The removal of such microbes may also have a positive effect on liver regeneration.

In summary, the present study demonstrated alterations in gut microbiota and liver metabolism during liver regeneration in HFD-induced MAFLD mice. Gut microbiota may influence the liver regeneration progression through metabolic pathways. MAFLD and liver regeneration were ameliorated by oral administration of A. muciniphila.

title: Gut microbiota dysbiosis promotes cognitive impairment via bile acid metabolism in major depressive disorder
text: AbstractEvidence suggests that complex interactions among the gut microbiome, metabolic abnormalities, and brain have important etiological and therapeutic implications in major depressive disorder (MDD). However, the influence of microbiome-gut-brain cross-talk on cognitive impairment in MDD remains poorly characterized. We performed serum metabolomic profiling on 104 patients with MDD and 77 healthy controls (HCs), and also performed fecal metagenomic sequencing on a subset of these individuals, including 79 MDD patients and 60 HCs. The findings were validated in a separate cohort that included 40 patients with MDD and 40 HCs using serum-targeted metabolomics. Abnormal bile acid metabolism was observed in patients with MDD, which is related to cognitive dysfunction. The following gut microbiota corresponded to changes in bile acid metabolism and enzyme activities involved in the bile acid metabolic pathway, including Lachnospiraceae (Blautia_massiliensis, Anaerostipes_hadrus, Dorea_formicigenerans, and Fusicatenibacter_saccharivorans), Ruminococcaceae (Ruminococcus_bromii, Flavonifractor_plautii, and Ruthenibacterium_lactatiformans), and Escherichia_coli. Furthermore, a combinatorial marker classifier that robustly differentiated patients with MDD from HCs was identified. In conclusion, this study provides insights into the gut-brain interactions in the cognitive phenotype of MDD, indicating a potential therapeutic strategy for MDD-associated cognitive impairment by targeting the gut microbiota and bile acid metabolism.Subject terms: Depression, Psychiatric disorders

title: Gut microbiota dysbiosis promotes cognitive impairment via bile acid metabolism in major depressive disorder
text:
Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a highly prevalent and recurrent condition, impacting over 350 million individuals globally [1]. Besides emotional symptoms, cognitive symptoms are also recognized as one of the core clinical manifestations of MDD and are also associated with a poor response to current antidepressant treatment [2]. Mood improvements do not necessarily translate into functional improvements. Deficits in executive function and attention might continue even when the emotional symptoms are completely alleviated [3]. Cognitive deficits that persist following the remission of depressive symptoms have been demonstrated to hinder the complete restoration of functional abilities, thereby resulting in increases in societal expenses allocated to the treatment of MDD [4].

Dysbiosis in the composition and functionality of gut microbiota may perturb immunological and metabolic pathways, contributing to the onset of psychiatric disorders, including MDD [5, 6]. Fecal microbiota transplantation using microbiota from MDD patients has been shown to induce depression-like behavior in mice, whereas probiotic supplementation can modify depression-like behavior in animal experiments [7, 8]. Population studies have also found that supplementation with probiotics, exercise, and dietary modifications can modulate the gut microbiota and potentially demonstrate antidepressant effects [9, 10]. In addition, other studies have demonstrated the causal role of the gut microbiome on cognition [11–13]. Gut microbial dysbiosis contributes to the development of various neurodegenerative disorders, which are often associated with cognitive impairment [14].

title: Gut microbiota dysbiosis promotes cognitive impairment via bile acid metabolism in major depressive disorder
text:
ion, other studies have demonstrated the causal role of the gut microbiome on cognition [11–13]. Gut microbial dysbiosis contributes to the development of various neurodegenerative disorders, which are often associated with cognitive impairment [14]. Studies have shown that probiotic supplementation can improve cognitive impairment in patients with MDD and Alzheimer’s disease (AD) [15, 16]. This dysfunction of microbiota-gut-brain axis is associated with various metabolic changes, involving the disruption of amino acid, energy, bile acid, carbohydrate, and lipid metabolism [5, 17–19]. Microbial metabolites are the connection and mediators between the gut and the brain; specifically, short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), secondary bile acids (BAs), fatty acid, and tryptophan play a critical role in metabolism. Some metabolites of the tryptophan pathway and SCFAs are depleted in patients with MDD [17, 20, 21]. Moreover, certain metabolites possess neuroprotective potential, including tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA), which could be involved in the prevention of AD [22, 23]. Upregulated microbiota-derived indoles can restore synaptic plasticity, and promote cognitive ability in an AD mouse model [24]. Microbiota and microbiota-derived metabolites modulate emotional and cognitive functions by regulating the permeability of the blood-brain barrier, cerebral energy homeostasis, and synaptic signaling [25].

The mechanism of cognitive impairment in MDD involves oxidative stress, neuroactive metabolites transmission, and other signaling pathways [26]. However, as of yet, there has been insufficient investigation into the impact of gut microbiota on cognitive function in patients with MDD.

text:

However, as of yet, there has been insufficient investigation into the impact of gut microbiota on cognitive function in patients with MDD. Most studies summarizing the evidence on the role of gut microbes and its metabolites in the development of psychiatric disorders, including MDD, do not refer to “cognition impairment” which is essential for the rehabilitation of social function [27, 28]. Two recent studies attempted to elucidate this matter using the 16S rRNA sequencing method; however, the sample sizes were limited and the studies primarily concentrated on the alterations in single “omics”, such as focusing on the analysis of gut microbiota composition while overlooking microbiota-derived metabolites, which serve as a critical conduit for the “cross-talk” between the brain and the gut microbiota [29, 30].

This study aims to address this knowledge gap. We conducted a multi-omics analysis of the gut microbiota and serum metabolome using data from 104 patients with MDD and 77 healthy controls (HCs). The changes in metabolomics were validated in another cohort that included 40 patents with MDD and 40 HCs. The multi-omics approach has the advantage of using multidimensional data which benefits the identification of biomarkers of cognitive deficits in MDD. The current study contributes to our understanding of the role of the gut-brain axis in the pathogenesis of cognitive impairment in MDD.

text: We further explored the mechanisms underlying cognitive impairment in MDD, examining the functions of the gut microbiota and BAs. We evaluated the impact of serum metabolomics, gut microbiota, and cognition. CIA revealed a stronger association between the serum metabolome and cognition (Fig. 6A) compared to the relationship between gut microbiota and cognition (Fig. 6B), potentially indicating the impact of gut microbes on cerebral processes via a more complex pathway, including the immune, endocrine, and nervous systems [43]. To further explore the effect of abnormal bile acid profiles on cognitive impairment in patients with MDD, LASSO regression was used to screen BAs that significantly contributed to cognitive function. BAs were found to contribute to several dimensions of cognitive function in patients with MDD, after accounting for age, sex, BMI, and degree of education (Supplementary Table 10). The results showed that gut-derived secondary BAs, including GLCA, GUDCA, and TUDCA, were related to cognitive impairment in patients with MDD. GUDCA and TUDCA were positive contributors to THINC-it Objective Cognition and THINC-it Composite Cognition, whereas GLCA was a negative factor (Fig. 6C, D). Taking each test separately as a dependent variable, the results showed that GUDCA was a positive predictor for Spotter, Codebreaker, Trials, and PDQ-5-D, whereas GLCA was a negative factor for Spotter and Trials (Supplementary Fig. 8). This indicates that GLCA, GUDCA, and TUDCA are correlated with several cognitive dimensions. The results also showed that GCDCA, a conjugated primary BA, was negatively correlated with THINC-it Composite Cognition, Trials, and PQD-5-D (Fig. 6C and Supplementary Fig. 8).

text:
Cognitive symptoms in patients with MDD respond poorly to widely used drugs that primarily act on 5-Hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) and norepinephrine (NE) receptors, suggesting that there may be other mechanisms underlying cognitive impairment. These results demonstrate that bile acid metabolism is significantly abnormal in patients with MDD, which is linked to changes in the gut microbiome and cognitive impairment. This study’s multi-omics data have, for the first time, identified a network of interactions within the gut-bile acid-brain axis in MDD patients with cognitive impairment. These findings provide a new therapeutic target for cognitive symptoms in MDD and suggest that the development of future probiotics or drugs to target bile acid metabolic pathways may be beneficial for cognition in patients with MDD.

Previous studies on the gut microbiome in depression have mainly focused on the severity of disease symptoms. Two studies using the 16S rRNA sequencing method, both characterized by small sample sizes, discovered alterations in gut microbes among patients with depression, suggesting possible impacts on cognitive function [29, 30]. Notably, our study employed metagenomic sequencing to identify microorganisms that exhibit a strong correlation with MDD, including Blautia_massiliensis, Anaerostipes_hadrus, Dorea_formicigenerans, and Fusicatenibacter_saccharivorans belonging to Lachnospiraceae; Ruminococcus_bromii; Flavonifractor_plautii; and Ruthenibacterium_lactatiformans from Ruminococcaceae and Escherichia_coli. These species exhibited a significant correlation with cognitive symptoms in patients with MDD.

These species exhibited a significant correlation with cognitive symptoms in patients with MDD. Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae, known for their role in butyrate and serotonin production, are considered beneficial microbes and be reduced in abundance in individuals with MDD [44, 45]. Gavaging rats with Escherichia_coli resulted in decreased serum estradiol and testosterone levels and induced depression-like behaviors [46, 47]. These results support our findings. Additionally, microbial dysbiosis is significantly correlated with cognition. Studies on age-related gut microbes found that the microbiota undergoes extensive changes; Faecalibacterium, Bacteroidaceae, and Lachnospiraceae are relatively reduced with aging and cognitive decline [48]. Ruminococcaceae, Lachnospiraceae, and Lactobacillus were found to be decreased in patients with AD, while Escherichia increased at the genus level in both fecal and blood samples from patients with MCI and AD [49, 50]. Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae, known to produce SCFAs, are the main predictors of hyperphosphorylated tau in AD [51]. Changes in gut microbes may contribute to cognitive impairment in MDD and a similar pathological process may occur in the above diseases with cognitive dysfunction.

Communication occurs bidirectionally between gut microbes and the brain through multiple pathways [52]. Gut microbiota convert and metabolize both dietary and host-originated compounds, producing a wide array of metabolites that exert local and systemic impacts. These metabolites are likely critical initiators of communication along the gut-brain axis [53].

Our results showed an increase in L-glutamic acid levels, which is consistent with findings that indicated elevated levels of L-glutamate in the postmortem brain tissue from MDD patients [56]. Elevated glutamate levels may play a role in the development of MDD by functioning as agonists at N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptor [57]. Ketamine, an NMDA antagonist, has been shown to exert rapid antidepressant effects [58]. Moreover, the neurotoxicity of excess glutamate has been demonstrated in neurodegenerative diseases [59, 60]. Recent research has reported that high levels of conjugated primary BAs and ammonia accumulation in the brain are correlated with cognitive impairment in age-related cognitive impairment [65]. GUDCA and TUDCA were strong positive contributors to cognition, whereas GLCA was a negative factor. In recent years, ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), GUDCA, and TUDCA have been recognized for their anti-apoptotic, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective properties. A wealth of experimental and clinical data implied their potential utility as modifying agents in the treatment of neurodegenerative disorders [66–68]. In general, these compounds elicit their therapeutic effects through the suppression of neuroinflammation, the attenuation of oxidative stress, and the preservation of mitochondrial integrity. Elevated secondary BAs synthesized by bacteria, as well as their conjugated derivatives such as deoxycholic acid, glycodeoxycholic acid, taurodeoxycholic acid, and GLCA, have been observed in individuals with AD [22].

These cytotoxic secondary BAs, including DCA and its conjugates, can alter the integrity of the blood-brain barrier and accumulate in the brain. Disruptions in bile acid metabolism contribute to metabolic diseases, including liver diseases, cardiovascular diseases, and diabetes, all of which have direct or indirect links to an increased risk of cognitive deterioration [69–72]. These collective findings suggest that the disruption of microbiota-bile acid crosstalk may promote inflammation and MDD disease phenotypes, including changes in cognition. Based on the current associative evidence, we hypothesized that microbiota manipulation and supplementation with anti-inflammatory BAs may hold promise as a therapeutic avenue for cognitive impairment in MDD.

The following limitations should be noted. First, untargeted analysis of serum metabolomics, in which most of the metabolites could not be identified, hampered our research. We focused only on metabolites known to be relevant to gut microbiota and the brain, such as BAs and neurotransmitter-like metabolites, and overlooking certain serum metabolites that might be vital in the pathophysiology of MDD, warranting further investigation. Although we validated our results in another cohort using targeted metabolomics, the metagenomic results could not be verified. Ideally, the verification of microbes should be performed in future studies with larger sample sizes. The potential influence of low-dose intermittent medication use on our results deserves careful consideration;

The potential influence of low-dose intermittent medication use on our results deserves careful consideration; although reports suggest that such doses and frequencies are acceptable, the results should still be interpreted with caution. Second, despite methodological corrections, the cross-sectional design could only establish a correlation between gut microbiota, metabolites, and cognition in MDD; therefore, a causality inference cannot be inferred. Further, longitudinal studies are required to clarify the roles of the microbiome and BAs in the cognitive symptoms of MDD. Thirdly, limited by the operability of cognitive assessment tools, we did not assess all dimensions of cognitive function, such as hippocampus-dependent memory. More comprehensive tools should be selected in future studies. Finally, the specific mechanisms underlying the role of gut-bile acid-brain axis disturbance in cognitive impairment related to MDD should be further clarified using fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) in animal studies.

In summary, our study has made several important contributions, namely identifying abnormalities of gut microbes and bile acid metabolism in patients with MDD, elucidating the interaction between the gut microbiome, bile acid, and cognition, and highlighting changes in microbial enzyme activity in the bile acid metabolic pathway. These findings clarify that the gut-bile acid-brain axis network may be correlated with cognitive impairment in MDD, providing new perspectives on the fundamental pathophysiological processes.

title: Gut Commensal Barnesiella Intestinihominis Ameliorates Hyperglycemia and Liver Metabolic Disorders
text: AbstractRecent studies have highlighted the role of the gut microbiota in type 2 diabetes (T2D). Improving gut microbiota dysbiosis can be a potential strategy for the prevention and management of T2D. Here, this work finds that the abundance of Barnesiella intestinihominis is significantly decreased in the fecal of T2D patients from 2‐independent centers. Oral treatment of live B. intestinihominis (LBI) considerably ameliorates hyperglycemia and liver metabolic disorders in HFD/STZ‐induced T2D models and db/db mice. LBI‐derived acetate has similar protective effects against T2D. Mechanistically, acetate enhances fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) through inhibition of histone deacetylase 9 (HDAC9) to increase H3K27 acetylation at the FGF21 promoter. The screening puerarin from Gegen Qinlian decoction in a gut microbiota‐dependent manner improved hyperglycemia and liver metabolic disorders by promoting the growth of B. intestinihominis. This study suggests that gut commensal B. intestinihominis and puerarin, respectively have the potential as a probiotic and prebiotic in the treatment of T2D.Keywords: acetate, fibroblast growth factor 21, gut microbiota, histone deacetylase 9, puerarin, type 2 diabetes

title: Gut Commensal Barnesiella Intestinihominis Ameliorates Hyperglycemia and Liver Metabolic Disorders
text:
Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is a chronic disease, characterized by hyperglycemia arising from insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency that affects more than 400 million people worldwide.[ 1 ] As the global prevalence of T2D has increased dramatically, there is an urgent need for enhanced prevention and management strategies.[ 2 ] The liver plays a key role in the maintenance of glucose homeostasis.[ 3 , 4 ] Liver metabolic disorders are risk factors for the development of T2D.[ 5 ] Under T2D conditions, liver dysfunction can lead to increased hepatic gluconeogenesis, inhibited glycogen storage, increased free fatty acids, and steatolysis, resulting in lipotoxicity damage.[ 6 , 7 ] Furthermore, hepatocellular injury and fatty changes in the liver aggravate glucose homeostasis.[ 8 ] These mechanistic findings are consistent with meta‐analyses showing that metabolic dysfunction‐associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) is a predictor of the development of peripheral insulin resistance and T2D.[ 9 , 10 ] Therefore, the improvement of liver metabolic disorders to combat T2D has become highly important.

Accumulating evidence has shown that the gut microbiota played a crucial role in the progression of T2D.[ 11 ] Manipulation of the gut microbiota may provide a new and safe therapeutic modality for combating T2D.

Accumulating evidence has shown that the gut microbiota played a crucial role in the progression of T2D.[ 11 ] Manipulation of the gut microbiota may provide a new and safe therapeutic modality for combating T2D. The dipeptidyl peptidase 4 from Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron degrades the glucagon‐like peptide‐1 (GLP‐1) to affect blood glucose homeostasis.[ 12 ] In contrast, supplementation with Clostridium sp could increase ursodeoxycholic acid levels to improve glucose intolerance by increasing GLP‐1 secretion.[ 13 ] The gut‒liver axis communicates mainly through the portal vein, which promotes bacterial messengers to regulate liver glucose and lipid metabolism.[ 14 , 15 ] Prevotella copri and Bacteroides vulgatus have been identified as the main species that drive the biosynthesis of branched‐chain amino acids, a group of metabolites that contribute to liver metabolic disorders.[ 16 , 17 , 18 ] An increased level of bacteria‐derived imidazole propionate deteriorates hepatic insulin resistance by activating rapamycin complex 1.[ 19 ] The gut microbiota produces secondary bile acids that improve hepatic inflammation, glucose, and lipid homeostasis via the farnesoid X receptor and the transmembrane G‐coupled protein receptor 5.[ 20 , 21 , 22 ] Thus, prevention of gut microbiota dysbiosis and restoration of homeostasis could be potential strategies for the prevention and management of T2D.

B. intestinihomini is an anaerobic obligate gram‐negative commensal, and few reports on the role of B. intestinihomini in T2D exist.[ 23 ] We demonstrated that oral administration of live B. intestinihomini significantly ameliorated hyperglycemia and liver metabolic disorders in HFD/STZ induced T2D model and db/db mice. Untargeted and targeted metabolomics, together with transcriptomics, revealed that B. intestinihomini‐derived acetate ameliorated T2D by increasing fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) in hepatocytes. Acetate inhibited histone deacetylase 9 (HDAC9) to increase H3K27 acetylation at the FGF21 promoter. The screened natural product puerarin promoted the growth of B. intestinihomini to ameliorate hyperglycemia and liver metabolic disorders in a gut microbiota‐dependent manner. Thus, treatment of B. intestinihominis as a probiotic and puerarin as a prebiotic agent might be promising strategies for treating T2D.

Intestinihominis in T2D Mice and PatientsTo identify the potential beneficial microbiome in T2D, a mouse model of HFD/STZ was utilized (Figure 1).[ 24 ] As shown in Figure S1A,B (Supporting Information), body weight did not differ among the chow and HFD/STZ groups. HFD/STZ significantly affected glucose homeostasis, as demonstrated by increased fasting blood glucose levels, serum insulin levels, homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA‐IR) index, and impaired oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) and insulin tolerance test (ITT) (Figure S1C–G, Supporting Information). In addition, T2D patients are usually accompanied by hypercholesterolemia and lipid accumulation in the liver. Increased liver weight, liver weight/body weight ratios, and serum aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels, total cholesterol (TC) and triglyceride (TG) levels indicated that HFD/STZ mice had hepatic steatosis and damage, as observed in H&E‐stained liver sections and a higher NAFLD activity score (NAS) (Figure S1H–N, Supporting Information). HFD/STZ did not affect α‐diversity (Figure S2A–C, Supporting Information), whereas principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) revealed a fecal microbial separation between the 2 groups (Figure 1B). HFD/STZ mice presented clear alterations at the phylum and genus levels and presented a higher Firmicutes‐to‐Bacteroidetes ratio (Figure 1C–E). To determine which gut microbiota members had a dominant role in T2D, we performed the linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe). At the genus level, the abundances of Allobaculum, Barnesiella, Clostridium_XlVa, and Bifidobacterium were decreased, whereas the abundances of Acetatifactor, Desulfovibrio, and Alistipes were increased in HFD/STZ mice (Figure 1F). Importantly, we found that the abundance of the genus Barnesiella was negatively associated with multiple metabolic parameters (including fasting blood glucose, HOMA‐IR index, OGTT, ITT, TC, and TG levels) (Figure 1G; Figure S2D–I, Supporting Information). We identified 3 species (B. intestinihominis, B.viscericola, and B.propionica) among the genus Barnesiella. LEfSe analysis revealed that the abundance of Barnesiella in the genus level and its species‐B. intestinihominis were decreased in the fecal samples from T2D patients, and a significantly negative correlation with the 2 h postprandial blood glucose (2hPBG) and Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) (Figure 1M,N; Figure S3C,D, Supporting Information). Additionally, our qPCR results demonstrated a significant decrease in B. intestinihominis abundance in the fecal samples from T2D patients (microbiota validation sets 1 and 2, Figure 1O,P; Figure S4 and Table S2, Supporting Information). Besides, we compared the fecal abundances of Barnesiella genus and B. intestinihominis in the GMrepo database.[ 25 ] The T2D patients had lower levels of Barnesiella and B. intestinihominis (Figure 1Q,R) than the healthy subjects. Intestinihomini Ameliorated Hyperglycemia and Liver Metabolic Disorders in HFD/STZ MiceTo investigate whether B. intestinihominis can alleviate hyperglycemia and liver metabolic disorders, HFD/STZ mice were treated with live B. intestinihominis (LBI) and heat‐killed B. intestinihominis (KBI) by daily oral gavage for 6 weeks (Figure 2A). Oral administration of LBI elevated B. intestinihominis level in the gut of HFD/STZ mice. The abundance of B. intestinihominis remained unaltered in KBI‐treated HFD/STZ mice (Figure 2B). Body weight did not differ among the chow, HFD/STZ, LBI, and KBI groups (Figure S5A,B, Supporting Information). Oral administration of LBI alleviated fasting blood glucose levels, serum insulin levels, the HOMA‐IR index, and OGTT and ITT results (Figure 2C–G). Furthermore, LBI treatment also reduced liver weight and the liver weight/body weight ratio and improved dyslipidemia (TG and TC) (Figure 2H; Figure S5C–E, Supporting Information). The plasma ALT and AST levels were significantly decreased by LBI (Figure S5F,G, Supporting Information). The NAS was higher in HFD/STZ mice compared to chow mice, indicating that HFD/STZ mice had liver steatosis and injury. Oral administration of LBI alleviated liver steatosis and injury in HFD/STZ mice (Figure 2I). However, KBI treatment had no effects on serum insulin levels, the OGTT and ITT results, liver weight, dyslipidemia, liver steatosis and injury, ALT and AST levels (Figure 2D,F–I; Figure S5A–G, Supporting Information). These findings indicate that LBI is beneficial and protective against hyperglycemia and liver metabolic disorders in T2D mice.Figure 2Oral administration of LBI attenuates metabolic disorder and gut barrier dysfunction in HFD/STZ mice.

Oral administration of LBI significantly decreased lipopolysaccharide (LPS) levels in serum (Figure 2J). Histological staining of colonic tissues revealed that, compared with HFD/STZ mice, LBI was able to maintain gut epithelial barrier function (Figure 2K). The epithelial expression of Occludin and ZO‐1 was significantly downregulated in HFD/STZ mice, whereas this suppression was reversed by the administration of LBI (Figure 2L–Q).2.4. B. Intestinihomini‐Derived Acetate Mirrored the Favourable EffectsWe performed untargeted metabolomics to evaluate the differential fecal metabolic profiles (Figure 3A,B; Figure S6A–C, Supporting Information). Twenty differential metabolites between the chow and HFD/STZ groups were identified by a variable importance in projection (VIP) ≥ 1.0 and a false discovery rate (FDR) of p < 0.05 (Table S3, Supporting Information). Oral administration of LBI significantly regulated 19 metabolites compared with HFD/STZ mice (Figure 3C; Table S4, Supporting Information). Notably, acetate was the most abundant and significantly enriched metabolite, correlated with most of the annotated top 5 KEGG pathways, such as pyruvate metabolism, glyoxylate, and dicarboxylate metabolism (Figure 3D; Figure S6D, Supporting Information).

The Wood‐Ljundahl pathway is the main pathway generating acetate by gut microbes.[ 31 ] Acetate is synthesized via 2 branches: 1) the C1‐body branch via the reduction of CO2 to formate and 2) the carbon monoxide branch via the reduction of CO2 to CO, which further combines with a methyl group to produce acetyl‐CoA. Acetyl‐CoA is catalyzed by the enzymes phosphate acetyltransferase (pta) and acetate kinase (ackA), with ackA controlling the ultimate production of acetate (Figure 3N).[ 27 , 32 ] We observed that the activity and expression of ackA were significantly increased after LBI administration (Figure 3O,P). Therefore, the decreased abundance of B. intestinihominis is more likely to lead to a reduction in acetate production.Incubation with acetate for 24 h significantly decreased hepatic glucose levels by inhibiting gluconeogenesis and increasing glycogen synthesis in PA‐induced primary hepatocytes, HepG2 cells, and HL‐7702 cells (Figure 4A–C; Figure S9A–H, Supporting Information). The administration of acetate decreased fasting blood glucose levels, insulin levels, and the HOMA‐IR index, and improved OGTT and ITT results in HFD/STZ mice (Figure 4D–I; Figure S10, Supporting Information). It significantly ameliorated liver metabolic disorders, as indicated by liver weight, liver weight/body weight ratio, pathological alterations, lipid content (TG and TC), and AST and ALT levels (Figure 4J–P). Acetate decreased serum LPS levels and improved the gut barrier structure in HFD/STZ mice (Figure 4Q–T).

text: the protective effect of acetate in PA‐induced HepG2 cells (Figure 5G–I; Figure S12D, Supporting Information), but HDAC9 siRNA significantly reversed gluconeogenesis, glucose consumption and glycogen synthesis in PA‐induced HepG2 cells (Figure 5J–L; Figure S12E, Supporting Information).Fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) is abundantly expressed in the liver and is closely associated with metabolic diseases.[ 33 , 34 ] Previous studies have reported that HDACs can upregulate the expression of FGF21 by promoting histone acetylation in the FGF21 promoter region.[ 35 , 36 ] In this study, B. intestinihominis and its derived acetate significantly upregulated FGF21 levels in HFD/STZ mice (Figure 5M,N; Figure S12F, Supporting Information). In PA‐induced HepG2 cells, we found that overexpression of HDAC9 abolished the upregulation of FGF21 by acetate (Figure 5O). Similarly, knockdown of HDAC9 upregulated FGF21 (Figure 5P). More importantly, ChIP‐qPCR analysis revealed that acetate upregulated histone H3K27 acetylation at the FGF21 promoter (Figure 5Q). Overall, these data suggested that B. intestinihominis‐derived acetate upregulated histone acetylation of the FGF21 promoter region and promoted the transcription of FGF21 by inhibiting the expression of HDAC9.2.6.Modulators that Ameliorated Hyperglycemia and Liver Metabolic Disorders were Screened by Promoting the Growth of B. title: Gut Commensal Barnesiella Intestinihominis Ameliorates Hyperglycemia and Liver Metabolic Disorders
section: The Reduced Abundance of B. Intestinihominis in T2D Mice and Patients
text:
To identify the potential beneficial microbiome in T2D, a mouse model of HFD/STZ was utilized (Figure 1).[ 24 ] As shown in Figure S1A,B (Supporting Information), body weight did not differ among the chow and HFD/STZ groups. HFD/STZ significantly affected glucose homeostasis, as demonstrated by increased fasting blood glucose levels, serum insulin levels, homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA‐IR) index, and impaired oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) and insulin tolerance test (ITT) (Figure S1C–G, Supporting Information). In addition, T2D patients are usually accompanied by hypercholesterolemia and lipid accumulation in the liver. Increased liver weight, liver weight/body weight ratios, and serum aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels, total cholesterol (TC) and triglyceride (TG) levels indicated that HFD/STZ mice had hepatic steatosis and damage, as observed in H&E‐stained liver sections and a higher NAFLD activity score (NAS) (Figure S1H–N, Supporting Information). These results suggested that the HFD/STZ‐induced mouse model mimicked the clinical phenotype of T2D patients.

We next performed 16S rRNA gene sequencing analysis on fecal samples from chow mice and HFD/STZ mice. HFD/STZ did not affect α‐diversity (Figure S2A–C, Supporting Information), whereas principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) revealed a fecal microbial separation between the 2 groups (Figure 1B). HFD/STZ mice presented clear alterations at the phylum and genus levels and presented a higher Firmicutes‐to‐Bacteroidetes ratio (Figure 1C–E). To determine which gut microbiota members had a dominant role in T2D, we performed the linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe).

title: Gut Commensal Barnesiella Intestinihominis Ameliorates Hyperglycemia and Liver Metabolic Disorders
section: The Reduced Abundance of B. Intestinihominis in T2D Mice and Patients
text:
lterations at the phylum and genus levels and presented a higher Firmicutes‐to‐Bacteroidetes ratio (Figure 1C–E). To determine which gut microbiota members had a dominant role in T2D, we performed the linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe). At the genus level, the abundances of Allobaculum, Barnesiella, Clostridium_XlVa, and Bifidobacterium were decreased, whereas the abundances of Acetatifactor, Desulfovibrio, and Alistipes were increased in HFD/STZ mice (Figure 1F). Importantly, we found that the abundance of the genus Barnesiella was negatively associated with multiple metabolic parameters (including fasting blood glucose, HOMA‐IR index, OGTT, ITT, TC, and TG levels) (Figure 1G; Figure S2D–I, Supporting Information). We identified 3 species (B. intestinihominis, B.viscericola, and B.propionica) among the genus Barnesiella. B. intestinihominis was significantly decreased in the fecal samples from HFD/STZ mice, and the abundance of B. intestinihominis was inversely associated with multiple metabolic parameters (Figure 1H,I; Figure S2J–N, Supporting Information).

Furthermore, we conducted shotgun metagenomics by 30 healthy subjects and 31 T2D patients from Nanjing Hospital of Chinese Medicine affiliated to Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine and found significant differences in the abundance of the gut microbiota. (Figure 1J,K; Figure S3A,B, Table S1, Supporting Information). LEfSe analysis revealed that the abundance of Barnesiella in the genus level and its species‐B. intestinihominis were decreased in the fecal samples from T2D patients, and a significantly negative correlation with the 2 h postprandial blood glucose (2hPBG) and Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) (Figure 1M,N; Figure S3C,D, Supporting Information).

Thus, B. intestinihominis may be related to the pathological progression of T2D.

title: Gut Commensal Barnesiella Intestinihominis Ameliorates Hyperglycemia and Liver Metabolic Disorders
section: Oral Administration of Live B. Intestinihomini Ameliorated Hyperglycemia and Liver Metabolic Disorders in HFD/STZ Mice
text: To investigate whether B. intestinihominis can alleviate hyperglycemia and liver metabolic disorders, HFD/STZ mice were treated with live B. intestinihominis (LBI) and heat‐killed B. intestinihominis (KBI) by daily oral gavage for 6 weeks (Figure 2A). Oral administration of LBI elevated B. intestinihominis level in the gut of HFD/STZ mice. The abundance of B. intestinihominis remained unaltered in KBI‐treated HFD/STZ mice (Figure 2B). Body weight did not differ among the chow, HFD/STZ, LBI, and KBI groups (Figure S5A,B, Supporting Information). Oral administration of LBI alleviated fasting blood glucose levels, serum insulin levels, the HOMA‐IR index, and OGTT and ITT results (Figure 2C–G). Furthermore, LBI treatment also reduced liver weight and the liver weight/body weight ratio and improved dyslipidemia (TG and TC) (Figure 2H; Figure S5C–E, Supporting Information). The plasma ALT and AST levels were significantly decreased by LBI (Figure S5F,G, Supporting Information). The NAS was higher in HFD/STZ mice compared to chow mice, indicating that HFD/STZ mice had liver steatosis and injury. Oral administration of LBI alleviated liver steatosis and injury in HFD/STZ mice (Figure 2I). However, KBI treatment had no effects on serum insulin levels, the OGTT and ITT results, liver weight, dyslipidemia, liver steatosis and injury, ALT and AST levels (Figure 2D,F–I; Figure S5A–G, Supporting Information). These findings indicate that LBI is beneficial and protective against hyperglycemia and liver metabolic disorders in T2D mice.

title: Gut Commensal Barnesiella Intestinihominis Ameliorates Hyperglycemia and Liver Metabolic Disorders
section: B. Intestinihomini Prevented Leaky Gut and Metabolic Endotoxaemia
text: Given that T2D is associated with leaky gut via the gut‐living axis,[ 15 , 26 ] we examined the effect of LBI on gut barrier functions in an HFD/STZ‐induced mouse model. Oral administration of LBI significantly decreased lipopolysaccharide (LPS) levels in serum (Figure 2J). Histological staining of colonic tissues revealed that, compared with HFD/STZ mice, LBI was able to maintain gut epithelial barrier function (Figure 2K). The epithelial expression of Occludin and ZO‐1 was significantly downregulated in HFD/STZ mice, whereas this suppression was reversed by the administration of LBI (Figure 2L–Q).

title: Gut Commensal Barnesiella Intestinihominis Ameliorates Hyperglycemia and Liver Metabolic Disorders
section: B. Intestinihomini‐Derived Acetate Mirrored the Favourable Effects
text:
We performed untargeted metabolomics to evaluate the differential fecal metabolic profiles (Figure 3A,B; Figure S6A–C, Supporting Information). Twenty differential metabolites between the chow and HFD/STZ groups were identified by a variable importance in projection (VIP) ≥ 1.0 and a false discovery rate (FDR) of p < 0.05 (Table S3, Supporting Information). Oral administration of LBI significantly regulated 19 metabolites compared with HFD/STZ mice (Figure 3C; Table S4, Supporting Information). Notably, acetate was the most abundant and significantly enriched metabolite, correlated with most of the annotated top 5 KEGG pathways, such as pyruvate metabolism, glyoxylate, and dicarboxylate metabolism (Figure 3D; Figure S6D, Supporting Information). Acetate is the end product of microbial fermentation in the gut.[ 27 ] Previous reports have revealed the benefits of acetate in attenuating metabolic diseases.[ 28 , 29 , 30 ] In this study, the fecal and liver tissue levels of acetate were significantly decreased in the HFD/STZ mice, while treatment with LBI significantly upregulated using GC‐MS‐Based targeted metabolomics (Figure 3E,F; Figure S7A,B, Supporting Information). Additionally, the fecal levels of acetate were inversely associated with multiple metabolic parameters (Figure S7C–H, Supporting Information).

Furthermore, we evaluated the differences in fecal metabolic profiles using untargeted metabolomics between healthy subjects and T2D patients and identified 19 differential metabolites (Figure 3G,H; Figure S8A–C and Table S5, Supporting Information).

title: Gut Commensal Barnesiella Intestinihominis Ameliorates Hyperglycemia and Liver Metabolic Disorders
section: B. Intestinihomini‐Derived Acetate Mirrored the Favourable Effects
text:
Furthermore, we evaluated the differences in fecal metabolic profiles using untargeted metabolomics between healthy subjects and T2D patients and identified 19 differential metabolites (Figure 3G,H; Figure S8A–C and Table S5, Supporting Information). Of note, the acetate levels were significantly decreased in the fecal samples from T2D patients, and acetate levels in T2D patients were also significantly lower than those in healthy subjects using targeted metabolomics (Figure 3I). Acetate levels were significantly correlated with B. intestinihominis, 2hPBG, and HbA1c (Figure 3J–L).

After 48 h of in vitro incubation with B. intestinihomini, acetate significantly accumulated in the supernatant compared with the vector control (Figure 3M; Figure S7I, Supporting Information). The Wood‐Ljundahl pathway is the main pathway generating acetate by gut microbes.[ 31 ] Acetate is synthesized via 2 branches: 1) the C1‐body branch via the reduction of CO2 to formate and 2) the carbon monoxide branch via the reduction of CO2 to CO, which further combines with a methyl group to produce acetyl‐CoA. Acetyl‐CoA is catalyzed by the enzymes phosphate acetyltransferase (pta) and acetate kinase (ackA), with ackA controlling the ultimate production of acetate (Figure 3N).[ 27 , 32 ] We observed that the activity and expression of ackA were significantly increased after LBI administration (Figure 3O,P). Therefore, the decreased abundance of B. intestinihominis is more likely to lead to a reduction in acetate production.

Incubation with acetate for 24 h significantly decreased hepatic glucose levels by inhibiting gluconeogenesis and increasing glycogen synthesis in PA‐induced primary hepatocytes, HepG2 cells, and HL‐7702 cells (Figure 4A–C; Figure S9A–H, Supporting Information).

text: ith acetate for 24 h significantly decreased hepatic glucose levels by inhibiting gluconeogenesis and increasing glycogen synthesis in PA‐induced primary hepatocytes, HepG2 cells, and HL‐7702 cells (Figure 4A–C; Figure S9A–H, Supporting Information). The administration of acetate decreased fasting blood glucose levels, insulin levels, and the HOMA‐IR index, and improved OGTT and ITT results in HFD/STZ mice (Figure 4D–I; Figure S10, Supporting Information). It significantly ameliorated liver metabolic disorders, as indicated by liver weight, liver weight/body weight ratio, pathological alterations, lipid content (TG and TC), and AST and ALT levels (Figure 4J–P). Acetate decreased serum LPS levels and improved the gut barrier structure in HFD/STZ mice (Figure 4Q–T). Taken together, these results indicate that acetate was the functional metabolite of B. intestinihominis that ameliorated hyperglycemia and liver metabolic disorders to combat T2D.
